clinicalPearls: A rare glomerular disorder defined by massive accumulation of type III collagen fibrils within the mesangium and subendothelial space of the glomerular basement membrane.
Characteristically presents with slowly progressive proteinuria, often nephrotic, with hypertension and gradual decline in renal function.
Serum levels of the aminoterminal propeptide of type III procollagen are markedly raised, providing a supportive circulating marker.
Distinct from nail-patella syndrome despite both showing glomerular collagen fibrils, as collagenofibrotic glomerulopathy lacks the nail, patellar and skeletal anomalies.
Both sporadic and familial forms are described, with some familial cases suggesting autosomal recessive inheritance.
Light microscopy shows enlarged glomeruli with a lobular, membranoproliferative-like appearance but immunofluorescence for immunoglobulins is typically negative.
Electron microscopy is diagnostic, revealing curved, frayed, banded collagen fibrils, best appreciated with phosphotungstic acid staining.
No specific therapy exists; management centres on supportive nephroprotection and control of blood pressure and proteinuria.
reference.pathophysiology: Collagenofibrotic glomerulopathy is characterised by abnormal deposition of atypical type III collagen fibrils within the glomerulus, predominantly in the subendothelial zone and mesangial matrix. Unlike normal collagen, these fibrils are laid down where they are not usually found and accumulate progressively, expanding the mesangium and thickening the capillary walls to produce a lobular, membranoproliferative-like architecture without true cellular proliferation. The circulating aminoterminal propeptide of type III procollagen is elevated, indicating dysregulated systemic type III collagen metabolism, although the precise defect in collagen synthesis, processing or clearance remains incompletely understood. Some familial clustering points to an inherited, likely autosomal recessive, disturbance of collagen handling, while sporadic cases also occur. The abundant fibrillar collagen distorts the filtration barrier and impairs glomerular haemodynamics, giving rise to progressive proteinuria and gradual loss of filtration capacity. Ultrastructurally the deposited fibrils are curved and frayed with a characteristic periodic banding, distinguishing the disorder from other fibrillary and collagen-related glomerulopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Nail-patella syndrome (glomerular collagen fibrils with characteristic nail, patellar and skeletal features)
Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (Congo red negative fibrils, immunoglobulin positive)
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
Phosphotungstic acid and type III collagen immunostaining to highlight the fibrils
Serum aminoterminal propeptide of type III procollagen
Congo red staining to exclude amyloid
Quantification of proteinuria and serial renal function
Clinical and radiological assessment for nail, patellar and skeletal anomalies to exclude nail-patella syndrome
Family history and, where relevant, genetic evaluation
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with progressive hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
Superimposed thrombotic microangiopathy in reported cases
Recurrence of proteinuria after kidney transplantation
reference.prognosis: The disorder generally follows a slowly progressive course, with many patients advancing to kidney failure over years, although the rate is variable. Prognosis is worse with heavy persistent proteinuria and poorly controlled hypertension.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lobular appearance for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis without performing electron microscopy
Confusing the condition with nail-patella syndrome despite the absence of extrarenal features
Overlooking the diagnosis when immunofluorescence is negative and dismissing the biopsy as non-specific
Failing to use phosphotungstic acid or type III collagen staining to demonstrate the fibrils
Assuming immunosuppression will help, when management is essentially supportive
references: Heptinstall's Pathology of the Kidney (standard reference)
Brenner and Rector's The Kidney (standard reference)
